title: Backstage — design
status: 2026-08-19 · Status: agreed direction, phased build. Constraining decisions live in [GDR-0006](../decisions/gdr/0006-app-never-phones-home.md) and [GDR-0007](../decisions/gdr/0007-backstage-web-lab.md); this document is the working design and may evolve.
html:
2026-08-19 · Status: agreed direction, phased build. Constraining decisions live in GDR-0006 and GDR-0007; this document is the working design and may evolve.

Backstage is Timbre's laboratory: a web app where every module of the product can be exercised, measured, and learned from — and, behind the same door, the website, the University, the feedback record, and eventually the customer list. It is also, explicitly, Hugo's AI-engineering curriculum: every layer is chosen to teach something the CV needs (evals, observability, tracing, RLS-backed multi-tenant data, modern full-stack).

1. The one hard rule

Everything below hangs off a single boundary:

┌──────────────────────────┐        artifacts, one direction only        ┌─────────────────────────┐
│  Timbre.app (macOS)       │  ─────────────────────────────────────────▶ │  Backstage (web)        │
│  zero network I/O, ever  │   eval JSON · dictation exports (opt-in)    │  SvelteKit + Supabase   │
│  GDR-0001, GDR-0006      │   GitHub issues · Stripe webhooks           │  Vercel + Langfuse      │
└──────────────────────────┘                                             └─────────────────────────┘

The app never phones home. Nothing in this design changes that. Data reaches Backstage only from the development side (timbre-eval, CI, imports Hugo performs) or from web interactions (site visits, purchases, feedback forms in a browser). "Analytics on for all users" is off the table, and so is "pay to turn analytics off" — the reasoning is in GDR-0006, summarized in §9.

2. Stack and what each piece teaches

Piece Role The lesson in it
SvelteKit 2 / Svelte 5 Site + Backstage app Modern reactive UI (runes), SSR, route groups, form actions
shadcn-svelte + Tailwind UI system Composition-over-library design systems
Supabase Auth, Postgres, RLS Real database modelling, row-level security, auth flows
Vercel Hosting, preview deploys CI/CD where every PR gets a URL
Langfuse LLM observability Traces, generations, scores, datasets — the eval vocabulary employers ask about
mdsvex University content Markdown-as-components, content pipelines
timbre-eval --serve Local lab daemon Service design; keeping one source of truth for logic

Node toolchain lives entirely inside web/ (pnpm, Node 22). Nothing outside web/ gains a JS dependency.

3. Monorepo layout

web/
  src/routes/
    (public)/                 marketing site: /, /download, /pricing
    (public)/university/      the University, sidebar navigation, mdsvex
    backstage/                gated: Supabase auth + owner allowlist
      lab/[module]/           module playgrounds (§5)
      evals/                  runs, cases, diffs over time (§6)
      feedback/               the feedback record (§8)
      customers/              CRM, Stripe-fed (§10, later)
    api/                      ingest endpoints (eval publish, feedback mirror)
  src/lib/components/ui/      shadcn-svelte
  src/lib/server/             supabase admin client, langfuse client
supabase/
  migrations/                 SQL, versioned, reviewed like code

Same repo, same review process: branch → PR → CI → squash. A web.yml workflow runs lint, svelte-check, and vitest on ubuntu runners (1× minutes, unlike the 10× macOS jobs) with paths: [web/**, supabase/**]. Vercel builds preview deployments per PR — review a UI change by clicking, not by imagining.

4. Auth and gating

The website and Backstage are one app. Public routes need nothing; everything under /backstage requires a Supabase session and an owner-role profile (single allowlisted email at first — signups exist for customers later, not for the lab). Gate lives in backstage/+layout.server.ts; there is no client-only auth anywhere. The University starts public: it is the learning-in-public artifact and the best marketing the site will have.

5. The module sandbox

The trap to avoid: reimplementing TimbreKit's logic in TypeScript so the browser can run it. Two implementations of SentenceTerminator will diverge, and then the lab tests fiction — the same sin as the synthetic corpus, one layer up. Also impossible for the model modules: FoundationModels and SpeechAnalyzer only exist on macOS; a Vercel function cannot run them.

So the lab keeps one source of truth: timbre-eval --serve, a local HTTP daemon mode on the Mac (port 4242) exposing the real Swift modules:

GET  /health                      → { version, model_available }
POST /polish                      → real TextPolisher (+ trace to Langfuse)
POST /terminate                   → SentenceTerminator
POST /spoken-commands             → SpokenCommands
POST /guardrail                   → PolishGuardrail verdict
POST /transcribe   (audio file)   → real Transcriber
POST /eval-run     (corpus id)    → full timbre-eval run, results persisted

Backstage lab pages probe localhost:4242. Daemon up → live playground against the real code (type a transcript, see polish/terminate/commands run, with per-stage latency). Daemon down → pages degrade to the recorded runs in Supabase. The daemon answers with Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network: true so a Vercel-hosted page may call localhost (Chrome PNA rules).

This is the design's best trick: the browser UI is universal, but the truth always executes on-device — the same property the product itself has.

6. Evals in Backstage

timbre-eval gains --publish: after a run, POST the results (corpus id, git SHA, prompt hash, repeats, per-case outcomes) to /api/evals with a service token. Backstage renders:

  • Runs over time — pass rate against git history: "did this prompt change help" becomes a chart, not a memory
  • Case drill-down — every output variant a case produced across repeats, failures highlighted
  • Diff view — two runs side by side, regressions in red

The 30%→47%→87%→98% arc from ADR-0004/0005 becomes the first recorded data.

7. Langfuse, in parallel and on purpose

Langfuse gets the trace-level view that Supabase tables don't model well, and it is deliberately redundant with §6 — the redundancy is the curriculum: build it yourself once (Supabase), use the industry tool once (Langfuse), and you can explain both in an interview.

  • Every /polish through the daemon emits a trace: input transcript → prompt assembly (app context, vocabulary) → generation (model output, latency) → guardrail verdict → terminator output.
  • Each corpus becomes a Langfuse dataset; each --publish run a dataset run with per-case scores (pass/fail per check).
  • Ingestion happens in web/src/lib/server/langfuse.ts via the JS SDK — the daemon posts to Backstage, Backstage forwards. One place holds the key; the Swift side never needs a Langfuse dependency.
  • Never from users' machines. Traces originate from Hugo's dev loop and CI only. Same boundary as everything else.

University module 14 teaches the concepts against this live wiring.

8. The feedback record

Feedback becomes a first-class record type, with GitHub issues as the canonical store (they already do threading, labels, state, and gh access):

  1. Something annoys you → dictate it (Timbre eating its own dog food) into gh issue create --label feedback
  2. A sync route mirrors feedback-labeled issues into the feedback table so Backstage can browse, tag, and link them to eval cases and releases
  3. A public /feedback form on the site (browser, not app) writes the same table for future users
  4. Feedback that changes direction still graduates to an ADR/GDR — issues record what happened, decision records record what we decided

First entry is already filed: the start-of-speech clipping found this morning.

9. Analytics and the "pay to disable" question

Asked and answered as a constraint, not a preference (full reasoning in GDR-0006):

  • In-app analytics for all users would make the app phone home. GDR-0001's "zero network requests" is a falsifiable claim — Little Snitch users will check — and it is the entire competitive wedge. Breaking it converts Timbre from "the one that never talks to the internet" into "another dictation app with telemetry."
  • Charging to turn analytics off prices privacy as a feature. In the one product category where privacy is the product, that reads as extortion, and "consent or pay" is legally contested under GDPR besides. Rejected.
  • What exists instead: server-side, cookieless page analytics on the website (a page_views table — you own the data, no consent banner needed); CRM populated by transactions (downloads, purchases, support threads — §10); and opt-in artifacts Hugo exports from his own machines.
  • Monetization charges for the product, never for silence.

10. Customers and payments (deferred phase)

Stripe Checkout on the site; webhook → customers table (email, product, license status). The honour-system commercial licence from the monetization discussion: free personal use, paid commercial use, license key delivered by email, no in-app enforcement ever — a licence check is a network call (GDR-0001/0006). The CRM is Backstage's customers view over that table plus feedback linkage: "this customer reported that issue" is one join.

11. Data model (v1)

profiles          (id → auth.users, email, role)         -- role: owner|customer
feedback          (id, source, body, app_context, github_issue, status, created_at)
eval_runs         (id, corpus, git_sha, prompt_hash, repeats,
                   cases_passed, cases_total, runs_passed, runs_total,
                   langfuse_run_id, created_at)
eval_results      (run_id, case_id, output, failures jsonb, passed)
dictation_samples (id, transcript, polished, app_context, recorded_at)  -- Hugo's opt-in exports only
page_views        (id, path, referrer, country, created_at)             -- no user id, no cookie
customers         (id, email, stripe_customer, product, status, created_at)

RLS: owner reads/writes everything; page_views and feedback accept anonymous inserts through server routes only (service role); customers see nothing (there is no customer-facing Backstage). Migrations are SQL files in supabase/migrations/, reviewed in PRs like any other code.

12. University migration

The single 91 KB HTML becomes mdsvex pages under (public)/university/ with a shadcn sidebar: 13 existing modules → one route each, prose intact; the original file stays in docs/learning/ as the historical artifact. field-notes.md stays in the repo — it's a dev-facing lab notebook, and its immutability-by-append matters; University pages may quote it.

New modules the growth plan already implies:

  • 13 · Evals in practice — the ADR-0004 story: properties over exact match, stochasticity, --repeat, the 30%→98% arc
  • 14 · LLM observability & Langfuse — traces, generations, scores, datasets; wired to the live §7 integration
  • 15 · The web stack, for someone who just learned Swift — runes vs @Observable, RLS vs sandboxing, the same concepts wearing different names

13. Phases

Phase Delivers Proof it works
0 (done today) This design, GDR-0006/0007, feedback issue #1 merged PR
1 SvelteKit scaffold in web/, shadcn, University migrated with sidebar, Vercel deploy, web.yml CI University readable at a real URL
2 Supabase project, auth, /backstage shell, eval publishing + runs browser 87%→98% arc visible as a chart
3 Langfuse wiring + traces, University modules 13–14 a polish trace inspectable end-to-end
4 timbre-eval --serve + live module playgrounds type into the browser, real Swift answers
5 Feedback mirror + site feedback form issue #1 visible in Backstage
6 Stripe, customers, downloads page first real licence sold

Each phase is one or more PRs; nothing lands unreviewed. Phase order is deliberate: the University ships first because it's the piece with an audience, and evals ship before playgrounds because recorded truth beats live toys.

14. Risks, named

  • The lab outgrowing the product. Backstage is infrastructure for Timbre; the roadmap's item 1 is still polisher quality. Time-box: if a phase doesn't serve shipping or learning, it waits.
  • Single maintainer, two stacks. Mitigated by the same review process, and by the daemon pattern keeping all product logic in one language.
  • Vendor surface (Supabase/Vercel/Langfuse). All three have exits (Postgres is Postgres, adapters swap, Langfuse self-hosts). Accepted for the learning value — using the real tools is the point.
  • Secrets sprawl. Service keys live in Vercel env + GitHub Secrets only. The repo rule stands: nothing secret is ever committed.

15. Where it stands (2026-09-25)

Backstage is the home, not just the lab: Overview (a dashboard read from the repo), Releases (the changelog), Decisions, Plans, Launch (the announcement copy and scripts, one Copy button away), Evals (every corpus case and the last measured run, with its git SHA), and the University — searchable from anywhere with ⌘K. Every page is fed by committed JSON that CI regenerates from the source files and fails on drift; the measured numbers are written by pnpm run measure on a Mac with the model. Phase 2's "eval publishing" therefore landed without Supabase: a recorded run in the repo is enough until there is a second machine producing them. Traces, Lab, Feedback and Customers remain phases 3–6 as above. The look follows GDR-0017.

title: The data inventory: what Timbre holds, where, and why
status: 2026-10-22 · Status: the record of processing for the app, the companion, iCloud sync, the website and the development side, kept current by the review (GDR-0030): a change that touches a row updates the row in the same pull request. Article 30 of the GDPR asks for this record; SOC 2's privacy criteria ask for the same facts. Where something is designed but not built, the row says so.
html:
2026-10-22 · Status: the record of processing for the app, the companion, iCloud sync, the website and the development side, kept current by the review (GDR-0030): a change that touches a row updates the row in the same pull request. Article 30 of the GDPR asks for this record; SOC 2's privacy criteria ask for the same facts. Where something is designed but not built, the row says so.

0. Who holds what

System Who holds the data Our role Processors
The Mac app, the iPhone app, the Watch app The user, on their own devices None: we never receive it. The user is the only holder. None. Apple's on-device frameworks process it on the device.
iCloud sync of the Library The user, in their own iCloud account None: the private CloudKit database is readable only by the user's devices. Apple, as the user's own provider under the user's iCloud terms.
The website and Backstage Hugo Pretorius, as the site's controller Controller Vercel (hosting, logs), Supabase (auth, database), GitHub (repository, issues, CI). Langfuse and Stripe are designed, not in use.
Development and release Hugo Pretorius Controller of his own material GitHub, Apple (notarisation, developer account), Anthropic (the review's model, under the maintainer's account).

1. The Mac app

Data Where Purpose Default Lifetime and erasure Leaves the Mac?
The Library: words, acronyms, phrases, spellings, corrections, each with a meaning, an example, provenance, tags, and the events strength is derived from; the profile (field, role, first language) ~/Library/Application Support/Timbre/library.json, one document written atomically Bias transcription, correct the polisher, answer explain, pick and practise the word of the day On: it is the product Until the user removes an entry (forgot is a tombstone), deletes the file, or uninstalls. Settings › Library shows every entry; Export writes the whole Library as one JSON file; Import merges. Only if the user turns on iCloud sync (§3)
Dictation capture: the date, the raw transcript, the polished text, the app name, the focused field's role and whether live typing was replaced, timings ~/Library/Application Support/Timbre/dictations.jsonl The user's own corpus; timbre-eval --import turns it into a corpus on the developer's own Mac only Off (GDR-0004) Until Delete All, from the same screen that turns it on; Show in Finder reveals the file Never
Microphone audio Memory, during a hold of the key On-device transcription with SpeechAnalyzer Granted by the user once Discarded as it is transcribed; never written Never
The pasteboard and the focused text field Memory, during one insertion Paste the result; replace the live-typed run Needs Accessibility, granted by the user Snapshot, set, paste, restore; nothing kept Never
The selection, for read-aloud and command mode Memory Read it aloud; fix, explain, shorten, plain Needs Accessibility Discarded after the command Never
The explanation card, the overlay, the word-of-the-day card Memory; the day's example sentence is kept in UserDefaults for the day Show the result On The card rebuilds daily Never
Settings UserDefaults for dev.hugopretorius.Timbre Preferences: reading speed, voice, toggles On Until the user resets them Never
The usage ledger: counts of dictations, words, commands, to-dos and readings, all-time and this week UserDefaults, key usageLedger The usage view in Settings On Reset from Settings; never a transcript, only counts Never
The word-of-the-day notification The system's notification centre, local The morning word Off (GDR-0027) Delivered and gone; no server Never
The update check: a GET for appcast.json on our site, and on Install a GET for the release zip from the same site Vercel's request logs (IP address, user agent, time) on the site's side Find a newer version; verify and install on request Off; a menu item, or a daily check the user turns on (GDR-0013); the download only on Install Vercel's log retention, not ours; no identifier, no query string, no cookie Yes: these are the only two requests the binary can make, both to our own site
Reminders The user's Reminders database (Apple), the "Timbre" list A spoken to-do lands in Reminders (GDR-0016) Asked for on the first spoken to-do The user's, in Reminders To the user's iCloud only if their Reminders sync; not through us

2. The iPhone and the Watch

Data Where Purpose Default Lifetime and erasure Leaves the device?
The Library The app group container group.dev.hugopretorius.Timbre Same as the Mac On Same as the Mac: Settings, Export, Forget Only with iCloud sync on
today.json: today's word, its strength and whether it was met The app group container, read by the widgets The widget, the Lock Screen, the complication show a word without reading the Library (ADR-0016) On Rewritten on every rebuild; deleted with the app Never
Hold-to-talk audio Memory On-device transcription with SpeechAnalyzer Granted once Discarded as transcribed Never
The Watch's text input Apple's system dictation and scribble UI A spoken to-do on the wrist Granted once Apple's Apple's dictation may use Apple's servers under the user's own Siri & Dictation setting; the Watch app does not yet say so (gap 4). Timbre adds nothing to it.
The to-do queue: each captured to-do's text and date pending-todos.json in the app group container on the Watch, then WatchConnectivity to the iPhone The Watch captures, the iPhone files (GDR-0029) On Each item stays in the file until the iPhone confirms it was filed; an item the iPhone never confirms stays until the Watch app is deleted, and there is no in-app way to drop it yet (gap 7) Watch to the user's own iPhone, through Apple's transport, never through us
Reminders The user's Reminders database As on the Mac; read-only on the Watch Asked once The user's As on the Mac
Settings UserDefaults on the iPhone and the Watch: the iCloud toggle (librarySyncsThroughICloud); on the iPhone also the day's example sentence (wordOfTheDayExample) Preferences On Deleted with the app Never

3. iCloud sync of the Library

Data Where Purpose Default Lifetime and erasure Who can read it
The Library's events and entries and the profile, as immutable records in the zone "Library" The user's private CloudKit database in container iCloud.dev.hugopretorius.Timbre The same Library on every device (ADR-0017) Off (GDR-0010) Until the user turns sync off and removes the app's data in their iCloud settings (System Settings › iCloud › Manage Storage). An in-app "delete from iCloud" is not built; see §6. The user's devices only. The private database is not readable by the developer. Encrypted in transit and at rest under Apple's keys. Not yet end-to-end encrypted: that needs the fields written as CloudKit encrypted values and record names that do not carry the term (gap 6).
Sync state ~/Library/Application Support/Timbre/library-sync.json on the Mac; library-sync.json in the app group container on the iPhone and the Watch Where CKSyncEngine left off; no personal data Off Deleted with the file or the app Never

Never synced, by rule: dictations, transcripts, captures, timings (GDR-0010). The schema is forever: no field renamed, retyped or removed.

4. The website and Backstage

Data Where Purpose Lawful basis Lifetime and erasure Status
Request logs: IP address, user agent, path, time Vercel Serve and secure the site; the same logs receive the app's update check Legitimate interest in running the site Vercel's default retention; not exported In use
Releases and the appcast Vercel, static files Distribute the app None needed: nothing is collected — In use
The University Served behind the lab's login (web/src/routes/backstage/university) The learning material None needed: nothing is collected — In use; a public University is the plan (backstage.md §4)
The Backstage login Supabase auth: one owner email (the maintainer's) and a session cookie Gate the lab The maintainer's own account Until the maintainer logs out or deletes the account In use; no public sign-up
Page views: path, referrer, country, time; no identifier, no cookie Supabase table page_views Know what is read Legitimate interest; no consent needed because no identifier is set Design: aggregate after 90 days, delete rows Designed, not built (backstage.md §9)
Feedback: body, app context, a GitHub issue number GitHub issues, mirrored to Supabase feedback Hear from users who choose to write Consent, by submitting the form Until the issue is closed and the row deleted on request Designed, not built (backstage.md §8)
Eval runs and results Supabase eval_runs, eval_results Measure the pipeline against synthetic corpora None needed: no personal data Kept as the measurement record Tables exist by migration (supabase/migrations/20260824120000_eval_runs.sql), empty; the publisher is not built
Dictation samples Supabase dictation_samples The maintainer's own opt-in exports, for evaluation The maintainer's own data Deleted by the maintainer Designed, not built; never anyone else's
Customers: email, Stripe customer id, product, status Supabase customers, Stripe Sell the product Contract Per the customer agreement, to be written Deferred
LLM traces Langfuse Debug the polisher's prompts on synthetic input None needed Per Langfuse's retention Designed, not built

The site sets no cookie for visitors. Behind the lab's login, two cookies exist for the one person who logs in: the Supabase session cookie, strictly necessary, and a sidebar_state preference cookie (seven days) set by the lab's sidebar. There is no consent banner because nothing needs one. A privacy notice for the site's logs and the lab's login is not yet published; see §6.

5. Development and release

Data Where Purpose Notes
The repository: code, records, design docs, the University, synthetic corpora, say-generated audio fixtures GitHub, public, under a LICENSE that reserves all rights The product and its book No real dictation, Library, email or screenshot of real data is ever committed (review C5). packages/TimbreKit/Fixtures/real-corpus.json, the import of the maintainer's own capture, is ignored by git. GDR-0005 still records the repository as private: the fact changed first and the record has not caught up (gap 5).
CI logs GitHub Actions Build and test on every pull request Build output only; no personal data in the corpora
The review evidence A review comment and a timbre/review status on each pull request; a local copy under .review/ (the pull request's JSON, the diff, the gate logs, the model's output), ignored by git, kept until the maintainer deletes it GDR-0030 The prompt sends the pull request's title, description, file list, gate results and diff to Anthropic's API under the maintainer's Claude account, and the model reads files from the checked-out tree. The public comment carries the head commit, the model and its cost, the maintainer's GitHub login and the time. No user data is in the repository, so none goes.
The release Apple's notarisation service receives the binary; the signed zip and appcast.json are published on the site Distribute a verified build The code requirement names the team; changing it strands every installed copy (ADR-0010)
Signing identities and secrets The maintainer's keychain; Vercel environment; GitHub Secrets Sign, deploy Never in the repository (review B4)

6. Rights, and the gaps

Right How it is met
Access (Art. 15) Settings › Library lists everything; the Library is one readable JSON file; captures are a readable JSON Lines file with Show in Finder
Portability (Art. 20) Settings › Library › Export writes the whole Library as JSON; Import merges it elsewhere
Rectification (Art. 16) The edit sheet on every entry
Erasure (Art. 17) Forget an entry (a tombstone that wins a merge), Delete All captures, delete the files, uninstall; iCloud through Apple's settings (gap below)
Objection and consent (Art. 7, 21) Every optional flow is off by default: capture, sync, update checks, the notification, Reminders access is asked on first use
Breach notification (Art. 33) No server of ours holds user data; the site's data is the maintainer's own and Vercel's logs

Known gaps, to be closed before the product takes customers:

  1. No in-app "delete from iCloud". The user can remove the app's data in their iCloud settings; the app should offer it in Settings › Library and call CKModifyRecordZonesOperation to delete the zone.
  2. No privacy notice on the site for Vercel's logs and the lab's login. Short, on the network page, before any form goes live.
  3. Processor agreements with Vercel and Supabase are their standard terms; record the versions accepted here when customers exist.
  4. The Watch's copy should say that the system's dictation is Apple's and may use Apple's servers under the user's setting, and its sync toggle should carry the same plain-words description the Mac's and iPhone's do.
  5. GDR-0005 still says the repository is private. It is public, under a LICENSE that reserves all rights; a record superseding that one sentence is pending, so the records, the inventory and the site agree.
  6. iCloud sync is not yet end-to-end encrypted. Advanced Data Protection covers only fields stored as CloudKit encrypted values and assets; the Library's fields are plain, and the event records' names carry the term. Before any user's zone exists: write the fields through encryptedValues and name records by an opaque hash, superseding ADR-0017's field list and GDR-0010's clause that the setting says "end-to-end encrypted when Advanced Data Protection is on". The copy says "not yet end-to-end encrypted" until then.
  7. An unfiled to-do on the Watch has no delete. pending-todos.json keeps an item until the iPhone confirms filing; the Watch should show the queue and let the user drop an item.

title: Timbre, the whole product
status: 2026-10-11 · Status: the map; its five decisions were taken on 2026-10-14 and are recorded in GDR-0023; GDR-0026 to GDR-0029 (2026-10-18) extend it to the Watch, the word of the day's bar, the bundled words, and the wrist's to-do key. Phases 1–5 are built (ADR-0013 to ADR-0017; the stack of pull requests from #64); their proofs on hardware are the next step. Constraining records: GDR-0001, GDR-0006, GDR-0010, GDR-0013. This document is where the product is planned as one thing; each piece that lands still gets its own record.
html:
2026-10-11 · Status: the map; its five decisions were taken on 2026-10-14 and are recorded in GDR-0023; GDR-0026 to GDR-0029 (2026-10-18) extend it to the Watch, the word of the day's bar, the bundled words, and the wrist's to-do key. Phases 1–5 are built (ADR-0013 to ADR-0017; the stack of pull requests from #64); their proofs on hardware are the next step. Constraining records: GDR-0001, GDR-0006, GDR-0010, GDR-0013. This document is where the product is planned as one thing; each piece that lands still gets its own record.

Timbre started as a key you hold to talk. It is about to become the place where the words you use get better: spelling, vocabulary, phrases, acronyms. This map lays out every piece, which surface owns it, where its data lives, and what crosses the one boundary the product is built on — so nothing is built twice and nothing falls between two surfaces.

1. Three pillars

Pillar What it is Today
Speak Dictate, fix/shorten/plain/explain, read aloud, say a to-do. Everything on-device, nothing leaves the Mac. Shipped (0.3.x, 0.4.0 forming)
Learn The Library — words, acronyms, phrases, spellings you are collecting — plus a profile that makes "explain" right for your industry, a word of the day, and practice that uses your own voice. Vocabulary, corrections and definitions exist as three Settings lists. Nothing else yet.
Run Backstage: releases, decisions, plans, evals, launch, architecture, brand. The business, in one place. Shipped

Speak is the wedge and stays the wedge: dictation that never leaves your Mac. Learn is the reason to open the app when you are not dictating, and the reason to want it on your phone. Run is ours.

2. Surfaces

Surface Owns Does not do
Mac app Everything in Speak. The Library's capture side: a word you taught, a correction, a definition, a word you had explained — each lands in the Library. The Mac is where words are met. Nothing cloud-side. Zero network requests (GDR-0001/0013).
iPhone app (planned) The Library in your pocket: review, practise, word of the day, add a word you heard. The phone is where words are kept. No dictation into other apps (iOS cannot), no commands. It is a companion, not a port.
Apple Watch app (planned, GDR-0026) The to-do key on the wrist; the word of the day on the face; Spell it; a word you heard. Deterministic, phone-optional. Anything that needs the model: that is the phone's or the Mac's, and arrives by sync.
Website The claim, the download, the network list. Accounts, sync, anything personal.
Backstage Running the product. Anything a user sees.
Cross-platform client (open) A Library on Android or the web, if ever. Only exists if there is an account to sign into — see §4.

3. The Library

One store replaces three lists. Every entry has a kind, and the kinds are exactly the four things Hugo wants to get better at, plus the one the app already keeps:

Kind Example Where it comes from What uses it
word ephemeral — short-lived explain on a word; added by hand; word of the day the polisher's vocabulary; practice
acronym ADR — Architecture Decision Record define in Settings; explain's answer, kept explain answers from it first (GDR-0012)
phrase a canary in the coal mine — an early warning explain on a selection; added by hand practice; the polisher leaves it intact
spelling definately → definitely fix corrected it; the spell checker fallback practice ("spell it"); a correction if it keeps happening
correction timber kit → TimbreKit taught in Settings; one day from your own edits CorrectionTable, before the model (GDR-0011)

An entry carries: the term, its meaning, an example sentence, where it came from (which app, dictated or typed, on which day), tags including the industry it belongs to, a strength that practice raises and time lowers (the spaced-repetition number), and its history. Nothing in an entry is ever transmitted by the Mac app; the entry is the user's.

Profile. Industry (one or more), role, first language. Used in two places: explain's prompt ("the reader works in healthcare, so PA means physician assistant before it means personal assistant"), and the word of the day's choice of lists. Lives in the Library, syncs with it.

4. The one boundary, and the sync decision

The Mac binary makes no network requests. That is the claim on the headline, falsifiable with a network monitor, and the entire competitive wedge (GDR-0001, GDR-0006, GDR-0013). The Library wants to be on the phone. There are two ways to get it there, and they are not equal:

A. iCloud B. A Timbre account
How CloudKit, private database, the user's own iCloud. Apple's daemons do the syncing; the binary still makes zero requests. GDR-0010 already accepted this shape for the dictionary. Supabase (already running Backstage's auth), the apps call it.
Reaches Mac and iPhone (and iPad, Watch). Anything with a browser.
Needs The iCloud capability on the App ID (done), a CloudKit container, an entitlement. No server, no cost, no account to create. Sign-up, sessions, a schema with row-level security, a privacy policy, GDPR handling, uptime.
Costs the claim Nothing. /network stays at one entry. The headline needs a second asterisk: the app phones home when you sign in. Amends GDR-0013; /network gains entries.
When it is right Now. When a non-Apple client is real and wanted — not before.

Recommendation: A first, and design the Library's store so that B is a second backend behind the same interface, not a rewrite. "Apple pure" is not a lite tier; it is the product. B becomes a decision the day there is an Android or web Library to sign into, and it gets its own record then.

5. Learning, using what Timbre already does

Practice should use Timbre's own abilities rather than becoming a flash-card app with a microphone bolted on:

  • Spell it. The phone shows the meaning; you say the word, then spell it aloud. The on-device recogniser hears both.
  • Say it. The phone shows a word or phrase; you use it in a sentence, out loud. The polisher's model judges whether it was used in its meaning — a guardrail-scored check, like every command (GDR-0012's rule for new verbs applies to new drills).
  • Explain it. The card you saw on the Mac, now a question: what does ADR stand for?
  • Word of the day. Chosen from the Library's weakest entries first, then from a bundled list for the profile's industry. Delivered as a local notification on Mac and iPhone. Saying it in a dictation that day marks it met. The bar it must clear is GDR-0027; where its facts come from is GDR-0028.
  • Gamification, the private kind. Strength bars, streaks, a weekly review. No leaderboard, no sharing, nothing that needs a server.

6. No gaps, no duplication

Capability Owner Store Sync
Dictation, commands, read aloud, to-dos Mac app — —
Capturing a Library entry from use Mac app Library (local) iCloud
Browsing, editing the Library Mac Settings → Library; iPhone Library iCloud
Profile iPhone and Mac, same screen Library iCloud
Practice, word of the day iPhone and Mac (a Practice window); the Watch for Spell it Library (strength, history) iCloud
Usage count Mac app UserDefaults never (GDR: this Mac only)
Dictation capture for tuning Mac app jsonl on disk never (GDR-0004)
Releases, decisions, plans, evals, launch, architecture, brand Backstage the repo CI

Shared logic lives in one place: the Library's model, parsing and practice scoring move into a platform-neutral TimbreCore package that the Mac app and the iPhone app both import; TimbreKit keeps the macOS-only pipeline. That split is a record of its own (an ADR) before the first iOS line.

7. Phases

Phase Delivers Proof
0 0.4.0: icon, disk image, to-dos, plain, live typing. Launch. Public.
1 The Library on Mac. One store with kinds; Settings › Dictionary becomes Library; explain, fix and define write to it; export to a file. Every existing list migrates; nothing lost.
2 TimbreCore + iCloud sync. The split (ADR-0013, ADR-0015), the CloudKit container and schema (ADR-0017), sync on two Macs. Teach on one Mac, see it on the other, nettop still empty.
3 Timbre for iPhone. The Library, profile, word of the day, Spell it. On the phone a minute after teaching on the Mac.
4 Practice that listens. Say it, Explain it, strength and streaks. A drill corpus the harness can score.
5 Profile-aware explain on the Mac. A commands corpus case per industry.
— Account and cross-platform. Decided when phase 3 has users asking.

GDR-0026 adds the Watch after phase 3: the to-do key first, because it needs nothing new; then the complication and Spell it.

8. Decisions this map asked for — taken 2026-10-14 (GDR-0023)

  1. Sync by iCloud first, account later or never (§4). Taken: iCloud first; the store built behind a sync interface.
  2. The iPhone app is a companion — the Library and practice — not a dictation app (§2). Taken: companion; no keyboard extension planned.
  3. One Library, five kinds, replacing the three Settings lists (§3). Taken: five kinds, migrated on the Mac first.
  4. TimbreCore split before the first iOS file (§6). Taken: created with the Library.
  5. Practice uses the voice — drills are scored like commands, with a corpus (§5). Taken: Spell it first.

title: The review: what every change is checked against
status: 2026-10-22 · Status: in force (GDR-0030). `tools/review.sh` runs this on the maintainer's Mac against a pull request and posts the evidence to it. Two readers: the human who merges, and the model the tool hands this file to. Both check the same list.
html:
2026-10-22 · Status: in force (GDR-0030). tools/review.sh runs this on the maintainer's Mac against a pull request and posts the evidence to it. Two readers: the human who merges, and the model the tool hands this file to. Both check the same list.

0. How the review runs

  1. Gates first, deterministically. Lint, the test suites of the packages the change touches, the Mac app and companion builds, the Backstage JSON drift check, the site's type check and build. A gate either passes or fails; nothing is judged.
  2. Then judgement, against this file. The model reads the pull request, its diff and the checked-out tree, and answers every section below. It returns findings with a severity, and the compliance answers of §4 and §5 as fixed fields, so the evidence is comparable from one change to the next.
  3. Then evidence, on the pull request. One review comment with the gates, the compliance answers, the findings and the identities (head commit, model, checklist version, tool version); inline comments where a finding has a line; a commit status timbre/review that branch protection can require.
  4. The human approves. The model never approves and nothing merges on its say-so. GitHub records who merged, and that record is the control.

The gates run on the Mac. The judgement runs through Claude Code on the Mac, which sends the diff and whatever files the model reads to Anthropic's API under the maintainer's own account. No user data is ever in the repository (§4, C5), so no user data goes.

1. Verdicts and severities

  • blocking — merging would ship a defect, break a convention that a record protects, weaken a user's right, or leave the inventory wrong. The verdict is changes needed.
  • should-fix — a real problem that can follow in the next change. The verdict can still be pass; the finding stays on the record.
  • nit — taste, naming, a sentence. Never changes the verdict.

A failed gate is blocking on its own.

2. Correctness and conventions

  • A1 · It does what the title says. The diff matches the description; no quiet widening or narrowing of scope.
  • A2 · The decision is extracted and tested. New behaviour follows the repository's pattern: a small nonisolated type with Swift Testing coverage (CLAUDE.md, Conventions). A behaviour with a right answer and no test is should-fix; a changed behaviour whose test was weakened to pass is blocking.
  • A3 · The conventions in CLAUDE.md hold. TimbreCore imports Foundation and Observation only; a package per framework with that framework's platforms; Swift 6 language mode and complete concurrency, opted into, never out of; no new @unchecked Sendable without the proof; no third-party dependencies; build settings in xcconfig, never the pbxproj.
  • A4 · Measured, not assumed. A change to a prompt, a guardrail or a corpus comes with its timbre-eval run, repeated (ADR-0004), in the description. One run is not a measurement.
  • A5 · Records. A decision that constrains future work has an ADR (a file) or a GDR (the product), immutable, superseding rather than editing. Numbers are taken from main at merge time, not from a branch.
  • A6 · Docs follow code. CLAUDE.md, the product map, the architecture model and the University are updated where the change makes them wrong; pnpm run sync:docs was run and the JSON is in the diff.
  • A7 · The user never loses an utterance. Any new path in the pipeline keeps the fallbacks: always paste something, never break focus, pasted text starts with a capital and ends a sentence.
  • A8 · Command mode never guesses and never destroys. A failure leaves the selection untouched.
  • A9 · A speech session is single-use; audio crosses isolation as AnalyzerInput; the converter is drained on stop.
  • A10 · Platform promises are checked against the SDK, not assumed from a framework's presence (GDR-0029).

3. Security

  • B1 · No new network path in the app. The binary makes no request except the opt-in update check to our own site (GDR-0006, GDR-0013). A new URLSession, socket, or framework that talks to a server is blocking.
  • B2 · Entitlements and permissions are the minimum. A new entitlement, usage string, TCC prompt or app-group access is named in the description with its reason. Changing the bundle identifier or the team is blocking unless a record says so (it orphans every grant and strands every update).
  • B3 · Updates trust the signature, not the website (ADR-0010). Nothing weakens the hash check, the code requirement or the notarization check.
  • B4 · Secrets stay out. No key, token, password or provisioning profile in the diff; nothing new reads them from the repository. Secrets live in Vercel's environment, GitHub Secrets and the maintainer's keychain.
  • B5 · The pasteboard and the focused field are handled as transient. Snapshot, set, paste, restore; read the field only to replace the typed run; never persisted, never logged.
  • B6 · Input from outside is data. Text from the pasteboard, the focused field, a transcript, a Reminders list, a CloudKit record or a web form is never executed and never trusted to carry instructions.
  • B7 · The site's gate holds. Everything under /backstage stays behind the owner role on the server; no client-only auth; anonymous writes go through server routes only.

4. Privacy and data protection

Personal data is anything about an identifiable person: dictated text, the Library, a to-do, a name, an email address, an IP address, a device identifier. Timbre's stance is that the user is the only holder of their data and we are not a controller of it, because we never receive it. The review keeps that true. The inventory in docs/design/data-inventory.md is the record of what exists; the GDPR calls it the record of processing (Article 30).

  • C1 · Does the change read, store, send, log or show personal data? If yes: which inventory row, for what purpose, and is it the least data that serves it (Article 5(1)(c), data minimisation)? A new store with no purpose line is blocking.
  • C2 · Is every new flow off by default and plainly described? Capture, sync, update checks and notifications are opt-in, described in Settings in plain words that match what the code does (GDR-0004, GDR-0010, GDR-0013). Consent that is bundled, pre-ticked or paid for is blocking.
  • C3 · Retention and erasure. Anything stored has a way to be deleted by the user from the same place it was turned on, and a stated lifetime. Anything synced through the user's iCloud is deletable there too (Article 17).
  • C4 · Rights are preserved. The user can still see everything the app holds (Article 15), export it in a usable form (Article 20), correct it (Article 16) and delete it (Article 17). A change that makes any of these harder is blocking.
  • C5 · No real user data in the repository. Corpora are written for the purpose; audio fixtures are generated by say; screenshots show the developer's own synthetic Library. A real dictation, a real Library, a real email in a fixture, a test or a document is blocking, and the file is removed from history, not just from the tree.
  • C6 · The copy tells the truth. Settings text, the website's claims and the record match the inventory. "Never leaves your devices" must stay literally true after the change (GDR-0010's honest-copy rule).
  • C7 · iCloud carries the Library and nothing else. Never a dictation, a transcript, a capture or a timing (GDR-0010's hard line). The schema is forever: no field renamed, retyped or removed (ADR-0017).
  • C8 · The site. A new field in a form, a new table, a new cookie or a new third party is named in the inventory with its purpose, its lawful basis, its retention and the processor's agreement. Cookieless by default; a cookie that is not strictly necessary needs consent that the site does not yet collect, so it is blocking until it does.
  • C9 · Apple's services are named for what they are. On-device speech and the on-device model are on-device; the Watch's system dictation may use Apple's servers under the user's own setting; iCloud is the user's provider. The copy says which is which.

5. Audit and SOC 2

SOC 2 reports on the controls an organisation operates, against the Trust Services Criteria; an auditor wants evidence that each control ran, every time, not a description of it. This process produces that evidence for change management, and checks that a change does not weaken the others.

  • D1 · Change management (CC8.1). Every change reaches main through a pull request with this review posted on it, the CI checks green, and a human merge. The review names the head commit, the model, the checklist version and the tool version, so the evidence is reproducible. A change that bypasses this (a direct push, a merge with a failed status) is a control failure to be recorded, not hidden.
  • D2 · Logical access (CC6). Who can merge, publish a release, sign and notarise, deploy the site and read the lab is a short list held by GitHub branch protection, the Apple Developer team, Vercel and Supabase roles. A change to any of those is a finding with the reason.
  • D3 · System operations (CC7). A release is built by tools/release.sh, notarised, hashed into the appcast and verifiable end to end by timbre-eval --verify-update. A change to the release path is reviewed with that proof in the description.
  • D4 · Confidentiality and privacy (C-series, P-series). The inventory is the statement of what is collected, why, for how long and for whom; §4 is how a change is held to it. Notice (P1), choice and consent (P2), collection (P3), use and retention (P4), access (P5), disclosure (P6), quality (P7) and monitoring (P8) all resolve to rows in the inventory.
  • D5 · Availability and integrity are the user's device's, not a service's; the product has no uptime to promise. The integrity control is that the pasted text is what was said and polished, measured by the corpora (A4).
  • D6 · The inventory is current. If the change touches a row, the row is updated in the same pull request. A stale inventory is blocking, because the whole stance rests on it.

6. What the model returns

A summary; a verdict (pass or changes needed); the compliance answers as fixed values — personal data (none, touched, new), network (none, dev side, site only, app), storage or logging (none, changed, new), third party (none, changed, new), real data in the repo (yes or no), user-facing copy (unchanged, changed and matches, changed and mismatches), rights (unaffected, preserved, weakened), inventory current (yes or no) — and a short note; then the findings, each with a severity, a category (correctness, convention, tests, records, security, privacy, audit, docs), a title, the detail, a suggestion, and the path and line in the new file where one exists.

Findings quote what the code does, not what it might do. A finding the model could not verify in the tree says so. Praise is not a finding.

7. What the human adds

The model has read the diff; the human has run the app. Before merging, the maintainer confirms the gates, reads every blocking and should-fix finding, runs anything the description claims was measured if the number looks surprising, and merges by hand. That merge, on a pull request carrying this review and green checks, is the control.
